renewal.note: HBO Max confirmed a two-season run. Season 2 debuted in December 2022 and concluded the story. Creator Alex de la Iglesia called it a complete narrative.

bollymeter.basis: Season 1 earned a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score from 17 critics on its US premiere; de la Iglesia's ability to blend village folk horror, Catholic mythology, and pulp genre craft into something genuinely singular was the near-unanimous verdict.

pull_quotes.text: 30 Coins is one of the most audacious horror series ever made - deeply weird, deeply Spanish, and deeply entertaining.

seasons.review_body: Season 1 of 30 Coins arrived as one of the most distinctive horror series European television had produced in years. Alex de la Iglesia - director of The Day of the Beast and El crimen ferpecto - brought his signature combination of Catholic dread, black comedy, and Grand Guignol practical effects to the HBO Max Spain framework and the result was something hard to categorise in the best possible way. The 100% Rotten Tomatoes score from 17 reviews on its US premiere reflected genuine enthusiasm rather than charity. Eduard Fernandez as Father Vergara anchored the series in something grounded enough to make the escalating supernatural horror land. The village-under-siege structure recalled great Spanish folk horror while the mythology felt genuinely original. Essential viewing for genre enthusiasts.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# 30 Coins S1E1: "The Coin" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

A baby appears where a calf should be, and the first instinct is not wonder. It is containment. Phones go away. Explanations are built before anyone understands the event. A town that wants order gets an impossible child, a priest with ritual knowledge, a woman ready to believe, and a coin that keeps pulling the hour away from village panic. "The Coin" works best when it treats the supernatural as a management problem. The horror starts because everyone thinks they can control the story.

## The Miracle Becomes Evidence

The sharpest idea in the premiere is that the strange event is treated like a public relations crisis. The line about nobody putting anything on Instagram until they know what it means is funny because it is practical, and frightening for the same reason. Before belief arrives, before doctrine, before terror, there is image control.

That gives **Paco** his clearest shape. He wants to keep order, stop the spread, and handle the baby responsibly. The episode does not strand him outside the madness as a passive official. It pulls him in because control is his weakness. Once the mystery exists, he keeps investigating, keeps checking, keeps trying to prevent escalation. Every responsible step takes him closer to the thing he cannot manage.

The Facebook beat is a smart escalation. The attempt to contain the event fails almost immediately because the town has already seen the photos. That is the episode's best modern touch: secrecy is treated as a tactic, not a guarantee. The supernatural event may feel ancient, but its first outbreak is social. The image of the baby is already ahead of the people trying to explain it.

That makes the premiere feel busy in the right way. It is dialogue-heavy because the town is trying to talk reality back into shape. The words do not calm anything. They multiply the problem.

## Easy as Pie, Until It Is Not

**Manuel Vergara** enters as the man with the kind of authority that should simplify the impossible. He identifies a swap. His phrasing, “and they swap the calf for the baby. Easy as pie,” is almost too casual, and that casualness is the point. The hour gives him the confidence of a person who has seen enough darkness to reduce it to procedure.

That is where "The Coin" starts to find its teeth. Manuel's authority is useful, but never clean. He frames events through confession logic, religious knowledge, and later the language of exorcism. When the priest's item is identified as the Catholic ritual for exorcisms, the episode shifts from civic confusion into spiritual danger. The show is not subtle about the turn, but bluntness suits the material. This is a premiere announcing its rules with a church bell, not a whisper.

The explanation of the swap risks flattening the mystery too early. The phrase lands with swagger, but it also tidies up a situation that is stronger when it feels less solved. The episode quickly has to re-complicate matters through the coin, the ritual object, and Carmen's attachment to the child. That works, but the middle stretch briefly mistakes a theory for momentum.

Manuel remains compelling because his solutions feel morally slippery. He does more than reveal truth. He manages people toward what he believes they can survive. That makes him valuable in a crisis and dangerous inside one.

## Carmen Turns Faith Into Possession

The baby is the premiere's emotional trap, and **Carmen** walks into it with terrifying conviction. She wants to keep and nurture the child as God-given. That belief drives the hour into violence.

Her refusal to give up the baby is where the episode stops treating the miracle as a puzzle and starts treating it as a contagion of certainty. The pleas around Antonio, the urgent commands to stop, and the repeated attempts to calm the situation create a scene built on people losing the ability to share the same reality. One side sees a child to be protected. Another sees a danger that must be interrupted. Nobody has enough proof, but everyone has enough fear.

This is the premiere's best escalation. The early crisis is handled through phones, public exposure, and local authority. By the time Carmen is told to come with the priest, the logic has changed. The town's social mechanisms have failed, so the episode pushes her into a religious and psychological frame. Voices, ritual, and obedience take over where explanation used to be.

The risk is that Carmen can feel more like a vessel for the episode's plot machinery than a fully opened character. Her desire is clear: keep the baby, believe in its divine meaning, act on that belief. The hour makes that desire strong enough to move the story, but it leaves part of her inner turn blunt. The crisis is legible. The human bridge into that crisis could be stronger.

## Blanks, Tricks, and the Cost of Control

The late reveal that Elena reports, “The bullets were blanks,” is the hour's most interesting reframe. It turns what looked like a lethal confrontation into a staged act of management. That matters because it confirms the premiere's governing idea: the real contest is over who gets to define reality for everyone else.

Manuel's staged approach can be read as protection. It can also be read as manipulation. The episode is smart enough to leave that discomfort alive. If the priest uses spectacle to contain a spectacle, has he solved anything, or has he shown how easily people can be moved? The open loop is strong because it is practical. His method works in the moment, but the hour plants the question of whether truth-management deepens the danger.

**Elena** functions as the person who names the deception after the fact, and that role gives the climax a necessary aftertaste. Without the blanks reveal, the sequence would play as pure supernatural panic. With it, the episode becomes nastier. Human planning is already inside the horror. Someone is staging, steering, and editing events while others mistake those events for divine proof or demonic fact.

Then comes the coin. The closing idea that it may be "just a piece of metal" gives the premiere its cleanest hook. The object does not need to explain itself yet. Its power is visible through behavior. People react to it, protect it, fear it, and build explanations around it. That is enough for a first hour.

## The Verdict

"The Coin" is a strong, overstuffed opener that understands the appeal of its premise: an impossible baby, a nervous town, a priest with dangerous competence, and an object whose meaning outruns the evidence. Its best craft choice is making the supernatural feel administrative before it becomes ritualistic. Phones, Facebook, official caution, confession logic, exorcism tools, staged bullets. Every system tries to contain the same rupture.

The unevenness comes from haste. Some mystery is explained too neatly before the hour has milked its dread, and Carmen's escalation needs more interior weight. Even so, the premiere plants sturdy questions. Who arranged the swap? What is the coin connected to? Is Manuel containing evil, or giving it a better playbook? The setup earns the next chapter.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A tense opener where the miracle is scary because everyone thinks they can manage it before it manages them.

episode_reviews.title: Judges
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season finale escalates to a scope that would embarrass many theatrical features, then pulls back to a human moment that grounds the mythology in actual stakes. De la Iglesia's control over his tonal range is remarkable.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final confrontation in the village square - staging that makes clear de la Iglesia was working at a scale HBO's budget genuinely supported.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 expanded the conspiracy mythology to global scale and Vatican intrigue; the ambition is compelling but the pacing is uneven compared to Season 1's concentrated village horror.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 moved 30 Coins off its village foundation and into a global conspiracy spanning Vatican City and Jerusalem. The scale expanded with the budget, and de la Iglesia filled the larger canvas with his customary invention. The season is more uneven than the first - the concentrated dread of Pedraza cannot be replicated once the story goes international, and some episodes feel like they are bridging rather than building. The mythology expanded to its logical extremes, and the conclusion provided genuine closure. The show remained far more interesting than most supernatural streaming fare.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 goes global and loses some of the village-horror claustrophobia that made Season 1 exceptional.
